newsitem.title: DUBAI: U.S. hostage remains holed up with Yemeni captors.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hostage remains holed up with Yemeni captors.

text.p: An American oil engineer kidnapped by a Yemeni mountain tribe remains holed up with his captors in the country's rugged interior, surrounded by security forces trying to win his release, industry sources said on Wednesday.

Joe D'ellaire, an engineer working for the U.S. engineering group Halliburton, was abducted on February 10 in Yemen's eastern Marib governorate by members of the Murad tribe, angered by a land dispute with Yemeni officials.

"He's still way up in the mountains. We haven't been able to get to him for days. We used to be able to get to him through our negotiator, but for the past couple of days we haven't been able to get to him at all," an oil industry source said.
"In part it's because the government troops are surrounding the area. They are being very careful about who they are letting in," he said.
Halliburton said on Tuesday they had been allowed to deliver food and clothing to D'ellaire through their negotiator. The company said the hostage appeared to be in a good condition.
The industry source said there had been no reports of violence between the troops and the kidnappers since the siege began on Sunday.

Security sources said the kidnappers were demanding compensation of $2 million or the return of a piece of land in the capital Sanaa they say was given to one of their tribal leaders, Sheikh Abdullah Abdrabu al-Mansouri.
The kidnappers, who are followers of Sheikh Abdullah, say land near the presidential palace had been donated to the tribal leader and later taken back by the Sanaa municipality.
Other leaders of the Murad tribe were also negotiating with Sheikh Abdullah's followers for the release of the American engineer, sources close to the negotiations have said.
They did not say whether the other tribal chiefs were leading the talks on behalf of the government.
D'ellaire was abducted from Rig 1 on the Saad al-Kamel oilfield, about 300 km (185 miles) east of Sanaa, oil industry officials said.

He was one of 125 men stationed on the rig, which belongs to Nabors Industries, a marketer of oil well drilling and oil field services. Halliburton had been hired to do special work for the private U.S. company Hunt Oil on the rig.
In recent years, Yemeni tribes with grievances against the government or foreign oil firms have kidnapped scores of tourists, diplomats or other foreigners to use as bargaining chips.
The hostages, who have included an employee of Hunt Oil and another from Nabors, were all released unharmed.
